sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ecgþēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: The house rendering of the speech formula, as at 529 and 631: ‘maþelode’ is the past of ‘maþelian’, the verb that opens a formal speech, and ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’ is ‘child of Ecgtheow’, ‘bearn’ (neuter nominative) in apposition to the name and ‘Ecgþēowes’ genitive. The colon opens Beowulf’s answer to Hrothgar’s long speech, which ended with the offer of treasure.

sentences.t: ‘Ne sorga, snotor guma!
sentences.l: ‘Sorrow not, wise man!
sentences.i: ‘Do not grieve, wise one!
sentences.n: ‘Ne sorga’ is a negative command: ‘ne’ with the imperative singular of ‘sorgian’, ‘sorrow, grieve’. ‘snotor guma’ is a vocative, ‘snotor’ a strong adjective, ‘wise’, and ‘guma’ ‘man’, so Beowulf is addressing Hrothgar directly and telling him to stop. The opening quotation mark is Klaeber’s, as printed in ‘t’.

sentences.t:
Sēlre bið ǣghwǣm,
þæt hē his frēond wrece, þonne hē fela murne.
sentences.l: Better it is for each, that he his friend avenge, than that he much mourn.
sentences.i: It is better for everyone to avenge his friend than to mourn greatly.
sentences.n: ‘Sēlre’ is the comparative of ‘gōd’ (‘better’; the OE comparative is formed from a different stem), a neuter predicate with ‘bið’, the form of ‘bēon’ that Old English uses for general truths, so this is a maxim. ‘ǣghwǣm’ is dative, ‘for each’. The ‘þæt’ clause is the subject and holds two subjunctives, ‘wrece’ (from ‘wrecan’, the verb used of the feud at 1333, ‘avenge’) and ‘murne’ (from ‘murnan’, ‘mourn’); ‘þonne’ here means ‘than’, and ‘fela’ is ‘much’. Beowulf answers Hrothgar’s lament with the duty of vengeance.

sentences.t:
Ūre ǣghwylc sceal ende gebīdan
worolde līfes;
sentences.l: Of us each shall abide the end of world-life;
sentences.i: Each one of us must wait for the end of life in this world;
sentences.n: ‘Ūre’ is the genitive plural of ‘wē’, ‘of us’, a partitive genitive with ‘ǣghwylc’, ‘each’, which is the subject. ‘sceal’ is ‘must’ (the necessity of death), ‘gebīdan’ ‘abide, wait for’, and ‘ende’ its object. ‘worolde līfes’ are two genitives, ‘of the world, of life’, which I read together as ‘life in the world’; the hyphenated ‘world-life’ in the literal version is mine, not a compound in the text.

sentences.t:
wyrce sē þe mōte
dōmes ǣr dēaþe;
sentences.l: let him work who may, of renown before death;
sentences.i: let him who may win glory before he dies;
sentences.n: ‘wyrce’ and ‘mōte’ are both subjunctive: ‘wyrce’ is a jussive, ‘let him work’ (from ‘wyrcan’), and ‘sē þe mōte’ is ‘he who may’ (‘mōtan’, ‘be able, be allowed’). ‘dōmes’ is genitive, which I take as the thing worked for (‘wyrcan’ with a genitive of what is won); that construction is a guess from the context. ‘dōm’ means ‘judgement, repute, glory’, the word on which Unferth’s failure turns at 1470. ‘ǣr dēaþe’ is ‘before death’, ‘dēaþe’ dative.

sentences.t:
þæt bið drihtguman
unlifgendum æfter sēlest.
sentences.l: that is for the troop-man, lifeless, afterward best.
sentences.i: That is the best thing for a warrior afterward, when he lives no more.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ points back to the renown just mentioned; ‘bið’ is again the general-truth form. ‘drihtguman’ is dative singular, ‘for the troop-man’ (the house rendering of ‘drihtguma’ at 99 and 1231), and ‘unlifgendum’ is a dative present participle with the negative prefix ‘un-’, ‘not-living’, agreeing with it: ‘for the warrior once dead’. ‘æfter’ is an adverb, ‘afterward’, and ‘sēlest’ the superlative, ‘best’.

sentences.t:
Ārīs, rīces weard, uton hraþe fēran,
Grendles māgan gang scēawigan.
sentences.l: Arise, guardian of the realm, let us quickly go, Grendel’s kinsman’s course to view.
sentences.i: Rise, guardian of the kingdom; let us go quickly and look at the track of Grendel’s kin.
sentences.n: ‘Ārīs’ is the imperative of ‘ārīsan’, ‘arise’, and ‘rīces weard’ a vocative, ‘guardian of the realm’ (‘rīces’ genitive; ‘weard’ is the house ‘guardian’ of 229 and 286). ‘uton … fēran’ is the hortatory ‘let us go’, ‘uton’ with the infinitive. ‘gang’ is ‘going, course, track’, the object of ‘scēawigan’ (‘look at’). ‘Grendles māgan’ is a genitive singular of a weak noun. ‘māga’ is ‘kinsman’ and masculine, and the masculine ‘hē’ at 1392 and 1394 agrees with it, so the literal version says ‘kinsman’; a feminine ‘māge’, ‘kinswoman’, would have the same ending, but I cannot confirm that noun in the lexica. The story makes the pursued creature Grendel’s mother (named at 1282; ‘hyre mǣg’ at 1339 is the kinsman she avenges), so the idiomatic version says ‘kin’, which fits either; why the text gives her masculine forms is not settled. That is a guess.

sentences.t: Ic hit þē gehāte:
sentences.l: I it to you promise:
sentences.i: I promise you this:
sentences.n: ‘gehāte’ is the first person singular present of ‘gehātan’, ‘promise’, with ‘þē’ the dative of the person and ‘hit’ the thing, anticipating the clause after the colon. The present tense carries the promise.

sentences.t:
nō hē on helm losaþ,
nē on foldan fæþm, nē on fyrgenholt,
nē on gyfenes grund, gā þǣr hē wille!
sentences.l: not will he into cover escape, nor into earth’s embrace, nor into mountain-wood, nor into ocean’s ground, let him go where he will!
sentences.i: The creature shall not escape into any cover, nor into the earth’s embrace, nor the mountain forest, nor the ocean floor; let it go where it will!
sentences.n: A run of negatives, ‘nō … nē … nē … nē’, ‘not … nor … nor … nor’. ‘losaþ’ is the present of ‘losian’, ‘be lost, escape, perish’, doing duty for the future. ‘on helm’ is ‘into cover’: ‘helm’ as ‘covering, protection’ (accusative after ‘on’, motion into); the apparatus records editors who read ‘holm’, ‘sea’, instead, and I follow ‘cover’ as a guess. ‘foldan fæþm’ is ‘the earth’s embrace’, ‘foldan’ a genitive of ‘folde’. ‘fyrgenholt’ is ‘mountain-wood’ (compare ‘fyrgenstrēam’ at 1359), and ‘gyfenes grund’ ‘the ocean’s bottom’ (‘gyfen’, ‘ocean’). ‘gā … wille’ is a subjunctive of concession, ‘let him go where he will’. Klaeber prints the masculine ‘hē’ both times; the apparatus lists editors who read ‘hē[o]’, ‘she’, since the pursued is Grendel’s mother, and I keep his text, which agrees with ‘māgan’ above, and say ‘it’ in the idiomatic version.

sentences.t:
Ðȳs dōgor þū geþyld hafa
wēana gehwylces, swā ic þē wēne tō.’
sentences.l: This day you patience have of every woe, as I of you expect.’
sentences.i: For this day have patience in each of your troubles, as I expect of you.’
sentences.n: ‘Ðȳs’ is the instrumental singular neuter of ‘þes’, and ‘Ðȳs dōgor’ is an instrumental of time, ‘this day’ (‘dōgor’, neuter, ‘day’); ‘hafa’ is the imperative of ‘habban’. ‘geþyld’ is ‘patience’, with ‘wēana gehwylces’, ‘of every woe’ (‘wēana’ genitive plural, ‘gehwylces’ genitive singular, ‘of each of woes’), saying in respect of what. In ‘swā ic þē wēne tō’ the ‘tō’ stands after its pronoun: ‘wēnan tō’ with the dative is ‘expect from’, so ‘as I expect of you’. The closing quotation mark ends Beowulf’s speech.

sentences.t:
Āhlēop ðā se gomela, Gode þancode,
mihtigan Drihtne, þæs se man gespræc.
sentences.l: Leapt up then the old one, to God gave thanks, to the mighty Lord, for that which the man spoke.
sentences.i: Then the old king leapt up and thanked God, the mighty Lord, for what the man had said.
sentences.n: ‘Āhlēop’ is the past of ‘āhlēapan’, ‘leap up’; ‘se gomela’ is a weak adjective used as a noun, ‘the old one’, Hrothgar. ‘Gode þancode’ takes the dative (‘þancian’ with the dative of the person), and ‘mihtigan Drihtne’ is a second dative in apposition. ‘þæs’ is a genitive, ‘for that’, giving what the thanks are for, and ‘þæs se man gespræc’ is ‘for what the man spoke’ (‘gespræc’ past of ‘gesprecan’), the man being Beowulf. The narrator reports Hrothgar’s thanks to God in his own voice; the king’s words are not quoted.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs Hrōðgāre hors gebǣted,
wicg wundenfeax.
sentences.l: Then was for Hrothgar a horse bridled, a steed twisted-maned.
sentences.i: Then a horse was bridled for Hrothgar, a steed with braided mane.
sentences.n: ‘wæs … gebǣted’ is a passive, ‘gebǣted’ the past participle of ‘gebǣtan’, which the lexica give as ‘bridle, put the bit in’ (a rare verb); ‘Hrōðgāre’ is dative, ‘for Hrothgar’. ‘wicg’ is ‘steed’, in apposition to ‘hors’. ‘wundenfeax’ is ‘wunden’ (twisted, braided) + ‘feax’ (hair), so a mane that is braided or curled; I give ‘twisted-maned’ in the literal version.

sentences.t:
Wīsa fengel
geatolīc gende;
sentences.l: The leader, the prince, splendid went;
sentences.i: The prince, their leader, set out in splendor;
sentences.n: ‘Wīsa’ is a weak noun, ‘leader, guide’ (the house rendering of ‘werodes wīsa’ at 259, not the adjective ‘wise’), and ‘fengel’ ‘prince, lord’: two nominatives in apposition for Hrothgar. ‘geatolīc’ is ‘splendid, fine’ (compare ‘gūðsearo geatolīc’ at 215), and I take it as agreeing with the subject. ‘gende’ is the manuscript’s form; the apparatus lists editors who restore ‘gen[g]de’, the past of ‘gengan’, ‘go’, as ‘gengde’ stands at 1412, and I read it as ‘went’.

sentences.t:
gumfēþa stōp
lindhæbbendra.
sentences.l: a men’s-foot-troop stepped, of shield-holders.
sentences.i: and a band of shield-bearing men marched behind him.
sentences.n: ‘gumfēþa’ is ‘gum’ (man) + ‘fēþa’ (a troop on foot, as the ‘fēþan’ of 1327), a nominative collective noun with a singular verb, ‘stōp’, the past of ‘stæppan’, ‘step, advance’. ‘lindhæbbendra’ is a genitive plural, ‘of linden-holders’, that is shield-bearers (‘lind’, linden wood, the shield; the house rendering of ‘lindhæbbend’ at 244 is ‘shield-holder’). ‘behind him’ in the idiomatic version is my addition from the sense.

sentences.t:
Lāstas wǣron
æfter waldswaþum wīde gesȳne,
gang ofer grundas, [swā] gegnum fōr
ofer myrcan mōr, magoþegna bær
þone sēlestan sāwollēasne
þāra þe mid Hrōðgāre hām eahtode.
sentences.l: Tracks were along the forest-paths widely visible, the course over the grounds, [so] directly she went over the murky moor, bore of the young-thanes the best, soulless, of those who with Hrothgar took thought for the home.
sentences.i: The tracks were plain to see far and wide along the forest paths, her course over the ground, where she had gone straight across the dark moor and carried off the best of the young thanes, lifeless, of those who kept watch over the home with Hrothgar.
sentences.n: ‘Lāstas wǣron … gesȳne’ is ‘tracks were visible’ (‘gesȳne’, an adjective, ‘to be seen’); ‘waldswaþum’ is ‘forest-tracks’ (‘wald’, forest, + ‘swaþ’, track; dative plural after ‘æfter’), and ‘gang ofer grundas’ restates the tracks. The bracket in ‘[swā]’ is Klaeber’s addition. The manuscript has ‘gegnū for’; the apparatus lists other fixes (‘þǣr hēo’, ‘hwǣr hēo’, ‘gegnunga’, ‘fērde’), and the whole clause is a guess in my reading: ‘gegnum’ I take as an adverb, ‘straight, directly’, and ‘fōr’ as the past of ‘faran’, ‘went’, with ‘she’ (Grendel’s mother) unstated. ‘myrcan mōr’ is ‘murky moor’. ‘magoþegna’ is a partitive genitive plural (‘young thane’ is the house rendering of ‘magoðegn’ at 407), ‘bær’ the past of ‘beran’, ‘þone sēlestan’ its object, and ‘sāwollēasne’ ‘soul-less’, i.e. dead, so Æschere is carried off. ‘hām eahtode’ is ‘took thought for the home’: ‘eahtian’ is ‘consider, esteem, deliberate’ in the lexica, and the sense ‘watched over’ is a guess; the apparatus lists Thorkelin (?) and Trautmann with ‘ealgode’, ‘guarded’.

sentences.t:
Oferēode þā æþelinga bearn
stēap stānhliðo, stīge nearwe,
enge ānpaðas, uncūð gelād,
neowle næssas, nicorhūsa fela;
sentences.l: Went over then the athelings’ child steep stone-slopes, narrow paths, constricted one-paths, unknown way, precipitous headlands, many water-monster-houses;
sentences.i: Then the son of princes went over steep stony slopes, narrow tracks, cramped paths for one at a time, an unknown way, sheer headlands, and many dens of water-monsters;
sentences.n: ‘Oferēode’ is the past singular of ‘ofergān’, ‘go over’ (‘ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’), and takes accusative objects, the list that follows. The verb is singular, so ‘bearn’ (neuter, nominative) is one person, ‘the child of athelings’ (‘æþelinga’ genitive plural), not a company; I take him to be Hrothgar, the same as ‘hē’ in the next line, but the text does not name him. ‘stānhliðo’ is ‘stone-slopes’, ‘stīge nearwe’ ‘narrow paths’ (the form could also be read as a singular, ‘a narrow path’), ‘ānpaðas’ ‘one-paths’ (paths wide enough for one, from the sense), ‘uncūð gelād’ ‘an unknown way’. ‘neowle’ is ‘steep, precipitous’ (the lexica give ‘prone, steep, deep’) with ‘næssas’, ‘headlands’. ‘nicorhūsa’ is a genitive plural after ‘fela’, ‘many’, and a kenning for the caves or lairs of the ‘nicor’, a water-monster.

sentences.t:
hē fēara sum beforan gengde
wīsra monna wong scēawian,
oþ þæt hē fǣringa fyrgenbēamas
ofer hārne stān hleonian funde,
wynlēasne wudu;
sentences.l: he, one of few, ahead went, of wise men, the plain to view, until he suddenly mountain-trees over grey stone leaning found, a joyless wood;
sentences.i: he went ahead with a few wise men to look over the ground, until suddenly he found mountain trees leaning out over grey rock, a joyless wood;
sentences.n: ‘fēara sum’ is an idiom, ‘one of a few’, i.e. ‘with a few others’; ‘wīsra monna’ is a genitive plural, ‘of wise men’, naming them; ‘beforan gengde’ is ‘went in front’. The subject ‘hē’ is not named; I take him to be Hrothgar. ‘wong scēawian’ is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to view the plain’. ‘oþ þæt hē … funde’ is ‘until he found’, with an accusative and infinitive, ‘fyrgenbēamas … hleonian’, ‘found mountain-trees leaning’. ‘fǣringa’ is ‘suddenly’, ‘hārne’ ‘grey’, and ‘wynlēasne wudu’ ‘joyless wood’ (‘wyn’ joy + ‘lēas’ without) is in apposition to the trees.

sentences.t:
wæter under stōd
drēorig ond gedrēfed.
sentences.l: water beneath stood, gory and troubled.
sentences.i: the water below stood bloodied and churned.
sentences.n: ‘wæter’ is the subject, neuter, ‘under’ an adverb, ‘beneath’, and ‘stōd’ ‘stood’. ‘drēorig’ is an adjective that the lexica give as ‘gory, bloody’ and also as ‘sad, dreary’; the next lines speak of blood, so I choose ‘gory’, a guess. ‘gedrēfed’ is the past participle of ‘gedrēfan’, ‘stir up, trouble’.

sentences.t:
Denum eallum wæs,
winum Scyldinga weorce on mōde
tō geþolianne, ðegne monegum,
oncȳð eorla gehwǣm, syðþan Æscheres
on þām holmclife hafelan mētton.
sentences.l: To all the Danes it was, to the Scyldings’ friends, in pain, in the mind, to be endured, to many a thane, a grief to each of the earls, after on the sea-cliff Æschere’s head they met.
sentences.i: All the Danes, the Scyldings’ friends, had to bear it in anguish of mind, many a thane, a grief to every earl, when they came upon Æschere’s head on the cliff above the water.
sentences.n: ‘Denum eallum wæs … tō geþolianne’ is ‘for all the Danes it was to be endured’: a dative of the person, ‘wæs’, and the inflected infinitive ‘tō geþolianne’, ‘to be suffered’. ‘winum Scyldinga’ is ‘to the friends of the Scyldings’ (‘wine’, friend, is a noun), and ‘ðegne monegum’ ‘to many a thane’, both in apposition to the Danes. ‘weorce on mōde’ is ‘in pain, in the mind’, ‘weorce’ the dative of ‘weorc’ in the sense ‘pain, grief’ (the exact construction is a guess); the apparatus lists a reading ‘wigum’ for ‘winum’ (Trautmann). ‘oncȳð’ is a noun, ‘grief’, in apposition, with ‘eorla gehwǣm’, ‘to each of the earls’. The clause ‘syðþan … hafelan mētton’ is ‘after they met (came upon) the head’, ‘hafelan’ accusative, ‘mētton’ the past plural of ‘mētan’. ‘holmclife’ is ‘sea-cliff’ (the house word at 230), here the cliff over the mere.

sentences.t:
Flōd blōde wēol — folc tō sǣgon —
hātan heolfre.
sentences.l: The flood with blood welled — the folk looked on — with hot gore.
sentences.i: The water welled up with blood — the people looked on — with hot gore.
sentences.n: ‘Flōd’ is the subject, ‘wēol’ the past of ‘weallan’, ‘well, boil’; ‘blōde’ and ‘hātan heolfre’ are datives, ‘with blood, with hot gore’ (‘heolfor’ is ‘gore’, as at 849). ‘folc tō sǣgon’ is a parenthesis between Klaeber’s dashes: ‘sǣgon’ is a past plural of ‘sēon’ (‘see’), and ‘tō … sēon’ means ‘look on’, so ‘the people looked on’.

sentences.t:
Horn stundum song
fūslīc f(yrd)lēoð.
sentences.l: The horn at times sang an eager army-song.
sentences.i: From time to time the horn sang out an eager battle-song.
sentences.n: ‘stundum’ is a dative plural used as an adverb, ‘at times’; ‘song’ is the past of ‘singan’. ‘fūslīc’ is ‘ready, eager’, agreeing with the song. The parentheses in ‘f(yrd)lēoð’ are Klaeber’s: the apparatus says the Thorkelin transcripts show ‘f’ and then a gap, and ‘fyrd-’ is Bouterwek’s restoration, so ‘army-song’ (‘fyrd’, army, + ‘lēoð’, song) is conjectural.

sentences.t: Fēþa eal gesæt.
sentences.l: The foot-troop all sat down.
sentences.i: The whole troop on foot sat down.
sentences.n: ‘Fēþa’ is the collective noun for a troop on foot, as in ‘gumfēþa’ at 1401, a nominative with the singular verb ‘gesæt’, the past of ‘gesittan’, ‘sit down, settle’; ‘eal’ is ‘all’. Whether they sit to wait or to watch the water, the text does not say.

sentences.t:
Gesāwon ðā æfter wætere wyrmcynnes fela,
sellice sǣdracan sund cunnian,
swylce on næshleoðum nicras licgean,
ðā on undernmǣl oft bewitigað
sorhfulne sīð on seglrāde,
wyrmas ond wildēor.
sentences.l: They saw then along the water many of the worm-kind, strange sea-dragons to try the swim, likewise on the headland-slopes water-monsters lie, which at morning-time often attend a sorrowful journey on the sail-road, serpents and wild beasts.
sentences.i: Then they saw many of the serpent kind in the water, strange sea-dragons swimming through the mere, and water-monsters lying on the slopes of the headlands, creatures that often at mid-morning keep watch on a sorrowful voyage over the sea, serpents and wild beasts.
sentences.n: ‘Gesāwon’ is the past plural of ‘gesēon’; its objects are ‘wyrmcynnes fela’ (‘fela’ with a partitive genitive, ‘many of the serpent kind’; ‘wyrm’ is serpent or dragon), ‘sǣdracan’ (‘sea-dragons’, a compound), and, as accusative-and-infinitive, ‘nicras licgean’, ‘water-monsters lie’. ‘sund cunnian’ is ‘try the swimming’, as at 1444. ‘næshleoðum’ is ‘headland-slopes’ (dative plural). ‘ðā’ is a relative, ‘which’, ‘on undernmǣl’ is ‘at undern-time’, with ‘undernmǣl’ an accusative after ‘on’ (‘undern’ is the morning, forenoon), and ‘bewitigað’ is the present plural of ‘bewitigan’, ‘observe, attend, watch over’; how the beasts attend ‘sorhfulne sīð’ (‘a sorrowful journey’) is not clear, and ‘keep watch on’ is a guess. ‘seglrāde’ is ‘sail-road’, a kenning for the sea (‘segl’ sail + ‘rād’ riding, road). ‘wyrmas ond wildēor’ names the creatures in apposition; Holthausen reads ‘wildor’ (apparatus).

sentences.t:
Hīe on weg hruron
bitere ond gebolgne;
sentences.l: They away fell, bitter and enraged;
sentences.i: They plunged away, bitter and furious;
sentences.n: ‘Hīe’ is the sea-beasts; ‘on weg’ is ‘away’ and ‘hruron’ the past plural of ‘hrēosan’, ‘fall, rush’. ‘bitere’ is ‘bitter, fierce’ and ‘gebolgne’ the past participle of ‘belgan’, ‘enraged’, both nominative plural.

sentences.t:
bearhtm ongēaton,
gūðhorn galan.
sentences.l: the noise they perceived, the war-horn sing.
sentences.i: they heard the clear note of the war-horn ring out.
sentences.n: ‘bearhtm’ is ‘a bright sound, clamor’, the object of ‘ongēaton’ (the past plural of ‘ongietan’, ‘perceive’); ‘gūðhorn galan’ is an accusative and infinitive, ‘the war-horn sing’ (‘galan’, ‘sing, sound’). The subject carried over from the last unit is the beasts, and the horn is the one that sang at 1423.

sentences.t:
Sumne Gēata lēod
of flānbogan fēores getwǣfde,
ȳðgewinnes, þæt him on aldre stōd
herestrǣl hearda;
sentences.l: One the Geats’ man from the arrow-bow of life deprived, of wave-strife, so that in his life stood the war-arrow hard;
sentences.i: A man of the Geats parted one of them from its life with an arrow from his bow, from the struggle in the waves, so that a hard war-arrow stood in its vitals;
sentences.n: ‘Sumne’ is accusative, ‘one’, the object, and ‘Gēata lēod’ the nominative subject, ‘man of the Geats’, who is not named; I take him to be Beowulf. ‘of flānbogan’ is ‘from the arrow-bow’ (‘flān’ arrow + ‘boga’ bow). ‘fēores getwǣfde’ is ‘deprived of life’: ‘getwǣfan’ takes a genitive, ‘fēores’, and ‘ȳðgewinnes’ is a second genitive, ‘of wave-strife’, which I read as ‘took it from the struggle in the waves’. ‘þæt him on aldre stōd’ is a result clause: ‘him’ is dative, ‘on aldre’ ‘in the life’, i.e. in the vitals, and ‘herestrǣl hearda’ ‘a hard war-arrow’ (‘here’, army). Klaeber ends with a semicolon.

sentences.t:
hē on holme wæs
sundes þē sǣnra, ðē hyne swylt fornam.
sentences.l: he in the water was in swimming the slower, because death took him.
sentences.i: It was slower at swimming in the water, because death took it.
sentences.n: ‘hē’ is the grammatically masculine creature just shot. ‘on holme’ is ‘in the water’ (‘holm’, sea, wave). ‘sundes’ is a genitive of respect, ‘in swimming’, and ‘þē sǣnra’ ‘the slower’ (‘sǣnra’, comparative of ‘sǣne’, ‘slow’, with the instrumental ‘þē’). I take ‘ðē hyne swylt fornam’ as ‘because death took him’, ‘fornam’ the past of ‘forniman’, ‘take away’; ‘ðē’ could also be read as a relative, and the choice is a guess.

sentences.t:
Hræþe wearð on ȳðum mid eofersprēotum
heorohōcyhtum hearde genearwod,
nīða genǣged, ond on næs togen,
wundọrlīc wǣgbora;
sentences.l: Quickly was on the waves with boar-spears, sword-hooked, hard hemmed in, by hostile assaults attacked, and onto the headland drawn, the wondrous wave-bearer;
sentences.i: Swiftly it was pressed hard in the waves with barbed boar-spears, set upon by savage attacks, and dragged onto the headland, that strange creature of the waves;
sentences.n: A passive built on ‘wearð’ with three past participles: ‘genearwod’ (‘narrowed, hemmed in’), ‘genǣged’ (‘assailed’, from ‘nǣgan’) and ‘togen’ (‘drawn’, from ‘tēon’). ‘mid eofersprēotum’ is ‘with boar-spears’ (spears for hunting boar), ‘heorohōcyhtum’ ‘sword-hooked’, i.e. barbed, a dative plural adjective agreeing with ‘eofersprēotum’ (‘heoru’, sword, + ‘hōc’, hook, + the adjective ending ‘-iht’), and ‘nīða’ ‘by hostile attacks’ (a genitive plural; the construction after ‘genǣged’ is unclear). ‘wǣgbora’ is a nominative, ‘wave-bearer’, a kenning for the beast (‘wǣg’ wave + ‘bora’ bearer); the apparatus lists ‘wǣgfara’ (Trautmann), ‘-dēor’ and ‘-þora’ as other readings. The dot under the vowel in ‘wundọrlīc’ (‘wondrous’) is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre; it is a mark on the printed text, not a different sound of the word. Klaeber ends the unit with a semicolon.

sentences.t:
weras scēawedon
gryrelīcne gist.
sentences.l: men gazed at the terrible guest.
sentences.i: The men stared at the dreadful intruder.
sentences.n: ‘weras’ is the plural subject, ‘men’, and ‘scēawedon’ the past plural of ‘scēawian’, ‘look at’. ‘gryrelīcne’ is an accusative adjective, ‘terrible’ (‘gryre’ terror + ‘-līc’), agreeing with ‘gist’, ‘guest, stranger’, here the beast washed up as an unwelcome visitor.

sentences.t:
Gyrede hine Bēowulf
eorlgewǣdum, nalles for ealdre mearn;
sentences.l: Girded himself Beowulf in earl-garments, not at all for life he mourned;
sentences.i: Beowulf armed himself in a warrior’s gear, and felt no anxiety for his life;
sentences.n: ‘Gyrede hine’ is the past of ‘gyrwan’ with the reflexive ‘hine’, ‘girded himself’, and ‘eorlgewǣdum’ the dative plural, ‘with warrior-garments’. ‘nalles’ is a strong negative, ‘not at all’, and ‘mearn’ the past of ‘murnan’, ‘be troubled, care’, with ‘for ealdre’, ‘about his life’. The line sets him against the other, who is identified at 1465 as Ecglaf’s son.

sentences.t:
scolde herebyrne hondum gebrōden,
sīd ond searofāh sund cunnian,
sēo ðe bāncofan beorgan cūþe,
þæt him hildegrāp hreþre ne mihte,
eorres inwitfeng aldre gesceþðan;
sentences.l: the war-byrnie, by hands braided, broad and cunning-adorned, was to try the swim, that could protect the bone-chamber, so that the battle-grip his breast might not, the angry one’s malice-grasp, his life harm;
sentences.i: His war-corslet, woven by hand, broad and cunningly patterned, was to try the water. It knew how to guard the body, so that the grip of battle, a furious foe’s treacherous clutch, could not harm his heart or his life;
sentences.n: The subject of ‘scolde’ is ‘herebyrne’, ‘army-byrnie, war-corslet’, feminine; ‘gebrōden’ is the past participle of ‘bregdan’, ‘braid, weave’ (the linked mail), and ‘hondum’ the dative plural, ‘by hands’. ‘sīd’ is ‘broad’ and ‘searofāh’ ‘cunningly adorned’ (‘searo’ craft + ‘fāh’ variegated). ‘sund cunnian’ is as at 1426. ‘sēo ðe’ is the feminine relative, ‘which’, and ‘bāncofan’ ‘bone-chamber’, dative or accusative (the weak endings coincide, and ‘beorgan’ takes the dative), a kenning for the body or torso (‘cofa’ chamber), the object of ‘beorgan cūþe’ (‘knew how to protect’). The ‘þæt’ clause is a result: the subjects ‘hildegrāp’ (‘battle-grip’) and ‘inwitfeng’ (‘malice-grasp’) share the singular ‘ne mihte’; ‘eorres’ is a genitive, ‘of the angry one’; and ‘gesceþðan’, ‘harm’, takes the datives ‘hreþre’ (‘breast’) and ‘aldre’ (‘life’).

sentences.t:
ac se hwīta helm hafelan werede,
sē þe meregrundas mengan scolde,
sēcan sundgebland since geweorðad,
befongen frēawrāsnum, swā hine fyrndagum
worhte wǣpna smið, wundrum tēode,
besette swīnlīcum, þæt hine syðþan nō
brond nē beadomēcas bītan ne meahton.
sentences.l: but the white helm the head guarded, that the mere-bottoms stir was to, seek the water-blending, honored with treasure, encircled with lordly bands, as it in days of old the weapon-smith made, with wonders equipped, beset with boar-likenesses, so that afterward no brand nor battle-swords could bite it.
sentences.i: but the bright helmet guarded his head, the one that was to stir up the depths of the mere and seek the churning water, adorned with treasure and ringed with lordly bands, as the weapon-smith had made it long ago, fashioned with wonders and set with boar-figures, so that afterward neither sword nor battle-blade could bite it.
sentences.n: ‘ac’ is ‘but’, passing from the corslet to the helmet. ‘hwīta’ is ‘white, bright’, ‘hafelan werede’ ‘guarded the head’ (as at 1327). ‘sē þe’ is a relative, ‘which’, and ‘meregrundas’ the ‘mere-bottoms’, object of ‘mengan’, ‘stir, mix’; ‘sundgebland’, ‘water-blending’ (‘sund’, swimming or the water swum in, + ‘gebland’, blending), is a rare word, compare ‘ȳðgeblond’ at 1373. ‘since geweorðad’ is ‘honored (adorned) with treasure’ (‘since’ dative), and ‘befongen’ ‘encircled’. ‘frēawrāsnum’ is a dative plural, ‘lord-bands’ (‘frēa’ lord + ‘wrāsn’ band); what the bands were on a helmet is a guess, perhaps a circlet or ridge. ‘swā hine fyrndagum worhte … smið’ is ‘as the smith made it in days of old’, ‘wundrum tēode’ ‘fashioned with wonders’. ‘besette swīnlīcum’ is ‘set with boar-likenesses’: boar-figures on helmets, as with the ‘eoferas’ of 1328. The last clause has the negatives ‘nō … nē … ne’ in agreement, ‘brond’ (‘brand’, sword) and ‘beadomēcas’ (‘battle-swords’) being the plural subject of ‘meahton’. The apparatus lists the reading ‘brogdne’ (Aant., Trautmann, Holthausen, Sedgefield) for ‘brond nē’, which would give ‘drawn battle-swords’.

sentences.t:
Næs þæt þonne mǣtost mægenfultuma,
þæt him on ðearfe lāh ðyle Hrōðgāres;
sentences.l: Not was that then the least of strength-helpers, that him in need lent the spokesman of Hrothgar;
sentences.i: It was not the least of helps in strength, what Hrothgar’s spokesman lent him in his need;
sentences.n: ‘Næs’ is ‘ne wæs’; ‘þæt’ is the subject, the sword about to be named, and ‘mǣtost’ the superlative of ‘mǣte’, which the lexica give as ‘small, mean’, so ‘least’. ‘mægenfultuma’ is ‘strength-helper’ (‘fultuma’ is a helper). The ‘þæt’ clause says what was lent: ‘him’ is Beowulf, ‘on ðearfe’ ‘in need’, ‘lāh’ the past of ‘līhan’, ‘lend’ (with the dative of the person). ‘ðyle Hrōðgāres’ is ‘Hrothgar’s spokesman’ (‘þyle’ is the house word, as at 1165), who is identified at 1465 as Ecglaf’s son (Unferth, as at 499 and 1165). Klaeber ends with a semicolon.

sentences.t: wæs þǣm hæftmēce Hrunting nama;
sentences.l: was to that hilt-sword Hrunting name;
sentences.i: that hilted sword was named Hrunting;
sentences.n: ‘wæs … nama’ is ‘the name was’, with ‘þǣm hæftmēce’ a dative of the possessor: ‘to that hilt-sword was the name Hrunting’. ‘hæftmēce’ is ‘hæft’ + ‘mēce’ (sword); the lexica give ‘hæft’ as ‘handle, hilt’ (it also means ‘bond’), and so ‘hilted sword’ is a guess at a rare word. ‘Hrunting’ is the sword’s name and stays untranslated; its derivation is not settled.

sentences.t: þæt wæs ān foran ealdgestrēona;
sentences.l: that was one foremost of old-treasures;
sentences.i: it was one of the foremost of ancient treasures;
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is the subject, the sword; ‘ān’ is the predicate, ‘one’, and ‘foran’ an adverb, ‘in front, foremost’. ‘ealdgestrēona’ is a genitive plural, ‘of old-treasures’ (the house rendering of ‘ealdgestrēonum’ at 1380), the group it stands first among.

sentences.t:
ecg wæs īren, ātẹrtānum fāh,
āhyrded heaþoswāte;
sentences.l: the edge was iron, with poison-twigs variegated, hardened in battle-sweat;
sentences.i: The blade was of iron, patterned with poison-twigs, tempered in the blood of battle;
sentences.n: ‘ecg’ is a feminine noun, ‘edge, blade’, ‘īren’ ‘of iron’. ‘ātẹrtānum’ is a dative plural of ‘ātor’ (‘poison’) + ‘tān’ (‘twig, sprig’), with ‘fāh’, ‘variegated, adorned’ (the word can also mean ‘stained’). What ‘poison-twigs’ were on a blade is a guess; the apparatus lists the conjectures ‘ātertǣrum’, ‘poison-drops’ (Cosijn, Aant.), and ‘ātertācnum’, ‘poison-tokens’ (Trautmann). The dot under the ‘e’ is again Klaeber’s mark for a vowel that does not count in the metre. ‘āhyrded’ is the past participle of ‘āhyrdan’, ‘harden’, and ‘heaþoswāte’ a dative, ‘battle-sweat’, a kenning for blood (‘heaþo’ battle + ‘swāt’ sweat, blood). Klaeber ends with a semicolon.

sentences.t:
nǣfre hit æt hilde ne swāc
manna ǣngum þāra þe hit mid mundum bewand,
sē ðe gryresīðas gegān dorste,
folcstede fāra;
sentences.l: never did it at battle fail any of men, of those who it with hands gripped, he who terror-journeys to undertake dared, the folk-place of perils;
sentences.i: Never did it fail in battle any man who closed his hands about it, any who dared to undertake terrible ventures and go to the field of perils;
sentences.n: ‘nǣfre … ne swāc’ is a double negative that is only emphasis; ‘swāc’ is the past of ‘swīcan’, ‘fail, betray’, with the dative ‘manna ǣngum’ (‘any of men’). ‘þāra þe hit mid mundum bewand’ is ‘of those who gripped it with their hands’ (‘bewand’, past of ‘bewindan’, ‘wind round, grasp’), and ‘sē ðe … dorste’ adds ‘who dared’. ‘gryresīðas’ is ‘terror-journeys’ (‘gryre’ terror + ‘sīð’ journey), the object of ‘gegān’, ‘go through, undertake’, and ‘folcstede’ is ‘battle-place’ (‘folc’ people + ‘stede’ place). ‘fāra’ I take as a genitive plural of ‘fǣr’, ‘danger’; it could also be a plural of ‘fāh’, ‘foe’, giving ‘the battle-place of foes’, and the choice is a guess.

sentences.t:
næs þæt forma sīð,
þæt hit ellenweorc æfnan scolde.
sentences.l: not was that the first journey, that it a valor-work perform should.
sentences.i: It was not the first time that it had to perform a deed of valor.
sentences.n: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘forma sīð’ ‘the first time’ (‘sīð’, journey, here an occasion), and the ‘þæt’ clause gives what happened: ‘æfnan scolde’ is ‘was to carry out’. ‘ellenweorc’ is the house ‘valor-work’ (as at 660 and 958), ‘deed of valor’ in the idiomatic.

sentences.t:
Hūru ne gemunde mago Ecglāfes
eafoþes cræftig, þæt hē ǣr gespræc
wīne druncen, þā hē þæs wǣpnes onlāh
sēlran sweordfrecan;
sentences.l: Indeed not remembered the son of Ecglaf, strong in might, what he before spoke, drunk with wine, when he that weapon lent to the better sword-warrior;
sentences.i: Surely Ecglaf’s son, a man of great strength, did not remember what he had said before, drunk with wine, when he lent the weapon to the better swordsman;
sentences.n: ‘Hūru’ is ‘indeed, certainly’, and ‘ne gemunde’ ‘did not remember’, ‘gemunde’ the past of ‘gemunan’; its object is the clause ‘þæt hē ǣr gespræc’, ‘what he spoke before’. ‘mago Ecglāfes’ is ‘son of Ecglaf’, nominative, i.e. Unferth, who is not named here; ‘eafoþes cræftig’ is ‘strong in might’ (‘cræftig’ is ‘strong, skilled’ in the lexica, ‘eafoþes’ a genitive of respect). ‘wīne druncen’ is ‘drunk with wine’ (compare ‘bēore druncen’ in Beowulf’s speech at 530). ‘þā hē þæs wǣpnes onlāh’ is ‘when he lent the weapon’: ‘onlēon’ takes a genitive of the thing, ‘þæs wǣpnes’, and a dative of the person, ‘sēlran sweordfrecan’, ‘to the better sword-warrior’, Beowulf. The text does not say which earlier words are meant.

sentences.l: himself not dared under the waves’ strife with his life to venture, lordship to perform;
sentences.i: he himself did not dare to risk his life beneath the strife of the waves, or to do a lord’s deed;
sentences.n: ‘selfa’ is the nominative ‘himself’, ‘ne dorste’ the past of ‘durran’ with two infinitives. ‘genēþan’ takes the dative of what is risked, ‘aldre’ (‘with his life’), and ‘under ȳða gewin’ is ‘under (into) the strife of the waves’ (‘ȳða’ genitive plural, as in ‘ȳðgewinnes’ at 1434). ‘drihtscype drēogan’ is ‘perform lordship’: ‘drihtscipe’ means ‘lordship, nobility, valor’ in the lexica, and ‘drēogan’ is ‘do, carry out’; the exact sense of the first word is a guess.

sentences.t:
þǣr hē dōme forlēas,
ellenmǣrðum.
sentences.l: there he lost renown, valor-glories.
sentences.i: and there he lost his name for courage and its glories.
sentences.n: ‘þǣr’ is ‘there, where’, and ‘forlēas’ the past of ‘forlēosan’, ‘lose’, which takes the dative: ‘dōme’ (‘renown’, as at 1387) and ‘ellenmǣrðum’, ‘valor-glories’ (‘ellen’ courage + ‘mǣrð’, a glorious deed, here dative plural). The apparatus gives the manuscript as ‘mærdam’ (the Thorkelin transcripts), with a Zupitza reading ‘: : rðum’; Klaeber prints ‘ellenmǣrðum’ without brackets, so the first half is his restoration.

sentences.t:
Ne wæs þǣm ōðrum swā,
syðþan hē hine tō gūðe gegyred hæfde.
sentences.l: Not was it with the other so, after he himself for battle clad had.
sentences.i: It was not so with the other, once he had armed himself for the fight.
sentences.n: ‘þǣm ōðrum’ is a dative, ‘with the other’ (Beowulf), and ‘swā’ ‘so’. ‘syðþan hē hine tō gūðe gegyred hæfde’ is a pluperfect, ‘after he had clad himself for battle’: ‘hæfde’ with the past participle ‘gegyred’ (from ‘gegyrwan’), and ‘hine’ reflexive. It answers ‘Gyrede hine Bēowulf’ at 1441 and closes the fitt.
